entries.text: "The KJV’s added words match the parallel verse in Chronicles. This comparison does not establish the translators’ intent or the italic marking of printed KJV editions; the packaged text contains no such markup. No claim is made about which of Samuel or Chronicles has the earlier wording, or whether two men named Goliath or two names for one man are meant. The Greek agrees with the Hebrew against the KJV, so both H and G apply. The Hebrew quoted is the Westminster Leningrad Codex digital text, with the consonants-only Aleppo-based edition as a second witness. A digital named edition is not proof that every manuscript agrees; other Hebrew manuscripts were not examined, and the KJV translators’ source for their wording is not established here. English glosses in brackets are the researcher’s plain renderings, not lexicon entries. The Greek is Brenton’s printed edition of the Septuagint."

entries.text: "The KJV matches the Greek of Mark here, so no G tag applies; this is a difference between Mark and 1 Samuel. Mark’s phrase could be read loosely as “in the lifetime of Abiathar, who was later high priest”, but 1 Samuel gives Ahimelech as the priest in office. Hebrew and Greek verse numbers in 1 Samuel 21 run one ahead of the KJV. The texts quoted are the Westminster Leningrad Codex digital text and a digital Textus Receptus; a digital named edition is not proof that every manuscript agrees."

entries.text: "G applies at Exodus 12:40 only, for the added words. The Greek of Genesis 15:13 agrees with the KJV and is quoted to show it. The numbers 400 and 430 can be reconciled if 400 is a round figure, or if the two counts begin at different points; none of the passages says so. Whether Galatians and Exodus can both stand depends on where the 430 years begin, which the KJV of Exodus states as the dwelling in Egypt. No claim is made about which form of Exodus 12:40 is original or about the actual length of any period. The Hebrew quoted is the Westminster Leningrad Codex digital text. A digital named edition is not proof that every manuscript agrees; other Hebrew manuscripts were not examined. The Greek is Brenton’s printed edition of the Septuagint, an ancient Greek translation tradition of the Old Testament. It is not a critical apparatus and does not show that all Greek witnesses agree or which reading is original. English in square brackets is the researcher’s plain rendering, not a KJV quotation and not a lexicon entry. The Greek New Testament wording is Tischendorf’s eighth edition as served by bolls.life (TISCH), compared with the Textus Receptus text served there (TR); neither is a critical apparatus."

entries.text: "No tag is proposed: the Hebrew and Brenton’s Greek agree with the KJV in both books. The two can be reconciled if the “clean fowls” of Deuteronomy 14:20 are meant to take in the leaping kinds that Leviticus allows; Deuteronomy does not name them or say so. They can also be reconciled if Deuteronomy gives a summary and leaves the exception to Leviticus; it does not refer to it. No claim is made about what these creatures are or about which law is older. entries.text: "Samuel names what was bought as “the threshingfloor and the oxen” and Chronicles as “the place”. If “the place” was a larger piece of land, two payments are possible; neither book mentions two. The owner is named differently in the two books; the record does not rely on that. The KJV matches the Hebrew in each book, and Brenton’s Greek of 2 Samuel 24:24 also has fifty shekels of silver, so no tag is proposed. The Hebrew quoted is the Westminster Leningrad Codex digital text. A digital named edition is not proof that every manuscript agrees; other Hebrew manuscripts were not examined.
